One exposure across several outcomes

Source: R/regression_outcomes.R
table_regression_outcomes.Rd

Fits one model per outcome, each with the same exposure and the same covariates, and shows the exposure's coefficients in one table: one row per outcome for a numeric exposure, one block of rows per outcome for a factor. The covariates enter every model and are named in the note, not shown in the table. Each outcome is fitted by stats::lm() or stats::glm(), as method and family say.

Usage

table_regression_outcomes(
  data,
  outcomes,
  exposure,
  covariates = NULL,
  method = c("lm", "glm"),
  family = stats::binomial(),
  complete_cases = FALSE,
  p_adjust = "holm",
  show_columns = c("n", "b", "ci", "p"),
  show_intercept = FALSE,
  labels = getOption("spicy.var_labels", FALSE),
  title = NULL,
  ...,
  note_labels = NULL,
  note = NULL,
  note_add = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A data frame. A survey design is refused with a pointer to the design-based route (class spicy_wrong_regime).

outcomes

The outcome columns, two at least (tidyselect, e.g. c(bmi, wellbeing_score) or starts_with("life_sat")). The exposure is not part of the selection: everything() and the other helpers skip it, and naming it is an error.

exposure

The exposure column (unquoted name, tidyselect): numeric, logical, a factor or a character column.

covariates

Covariate columns entered in every model (tidyselect), or NULL (default) for unadjusted models. The exposure and the outcomes are not part of the selection.

method

The model fitted for every outcome: "lm" (default) or "glm". Not combined with a list of families. See Which model for which outcome.

family

The family of the glm: one family for every outcome (default binomial(), used when method = "glm"; typing a family alone selects glm()), or a named list giving a family to some outcomes, the others fitted by lm(). See Which model for which outcome.

complete_cases

Logical, default FALSE. TRUE fits every model on the rows complete on all the outcomes, the exposure and the covariates. See Sample sizes.

p_adjust

The adjustment of the p-values for multiple testing, across the exposure rows of all the models: "holm" (default), "none", or any other method of stats::p.adjust(). See Multiplicity.

show_columns

Passed to table_regression(). Default c("n", "b", "ci", "p"); "n" is the sample size of each model. "r2" and "adj_r2" give each outcome's own model R-squared (linear models), next to its N. The AME columns and "none" are refused.

show_intercept

Display the (Intercept) row of each model? Default FALSE. See Intercepts.

labels

How the variables are named: an outcome in its row or at the head of its block, the exposure in the title and on its rows, a covariate in the note. The four forms of table_regression(): FALSE (the column names), TRUE (each column's label attribute when it has one), a named character vector, or var_labels(). The names are the columns and the coefficient names ("sexMale" names the row of one level, in every block). The default reads options(spicy.var_labels).

title

Table title; NULL (default) names the model when every outcome has the same ("Linear regression of each outcome on <exposure>", "Logistic regression of each outcome on <exposure>"), else "Regression of each outcome on <exposure>".

...

Passed to table_regression() (exponentiate, vcov, cluster, ci_level, digits, output, ...), each by its full name: an unknown or abbreviated name is an error. nested, layout, keep, drop, factor_layout = "flat", outcome_labels and standardized do not apply to a table of outcomes and are refused. cluster must be a single vector with one value per row of data; it is aligned to each model's own estimation sample.

note_labels

A named character vector giving the exposure (in the title) and the covariates (in the note) a label of their own. The outcomes are named in the rows and take none.

note

The note under the table. NULL (the default) builds it: the general note, one paragraph opened by the lead-in of the style ("Note." by default, none under the jama and lancet themes; see note_label in spicy_style()), then, in a table_regression() with stars, the legend of the stars on a line of its own. A single string replaces the general note, the sentences the table writes about its data included. It is printed as typed, line breaks ("\n") included, after the lead-in of the style, which a string opening with a lead-in of its own does not repeat (note = "Note. Data weighted."), and the legend of the stars stays below it. "" keeps that legend alone, and no note at all without stars. FALSE removes the note from every output, the legend included.

note_add

Sentences to add to the note: a character vector of one or more strings, each printed as typed (no period is added) and joined to the note by a space. They close its paragraph, after the definitions of the abbreviations and before the legend of the stars, in every output and in attr(x, "note"), and the sentences the table writes stay. With a string in note, they follow it, so a wrapper can add a house sentence to every table while one table replaces its note. An NA or an empty string is an error, and so is note_add with note = FALSE, which leaves no note to add to.

Value

See table_regression() (same output contract). The first column is headed "Outcome". tidy() and output = "long" give one row per outcome and coefficient of the exposure, named as R names the coefficient, with the outcome in the outcome column and whether the estimate is exponentiated in exponentiated. glance() gives one row per outcome, the fit statistics of its model.

Which model for which outcome

The function does not guess a model from the type of an outcome: it fits what method and family say.

You typeModels
neither method nor familyevery outcome by lm()
method = "glm"every outcome by glm(), family = binomial()
family = poisson() (one family)every outcome by glm() with that family
family = list(smoking = binomial(), visits = poisson())the named outcomes by glm(), the others by lm()
a list and methodan error: the list already says which outcomes are glm

A family is given in any form stats::glm() takes: the object, its name or its constructor, in a list as alone. A name of the list that is not an outcome is an error, and so is gaussian() with the identity link (leave that outcome out of the list: it is then fitted by lm()). A two-level outcome (a factor, a logical, or 0/1) fitted by lm() is a linear probability model of its second level, and a warning says so unless method = "lm" was typed.

Scales

exponentiate = TRUE exponentiates the blocks of the glm with a log or logit link (odds ratios, rate ratios) and leaves the linear models on their scale. When every block has the same measure, the column is headed by it ("B", "OR", "IRR"). When the measures differ, the column is headed "Estimate" and each outcome names its own ("smoking (OR)", "bmi (B)"); the note says which models are exponentiated. tidy() and output = "long" say it row by row in their exponentiated column. The "t" column is refused when linear models and glm mix: it would hold a t for some rows and a z for others.

Sample sizes

By default each model is fit on its own complete cases (its outcome, the exposure and the covariates), so N can vary across outcomes. The N column shows each model's N on the row of its outcome, or on the header of its block (the line that names the outcome) when the outcome has several rows, and the note gives the range whenever the Ns differ. The R-squared columns are placed the same way. Pass complete_cases = TRUE to fit every model on the rows complete on all the outcomes, the exposure and the covariates; the note then gives that common N.

Multiplicity

The p-values are adjusted by default (p_adjust = "holm"), across the exposure rows of every model taken as one family: k tests for a numeric exposure and k outcomes, k x (L - 1) for a factor of L levels. The covariates and the intercepts are not part of the family. The note counts the outcomes and the tests. p_adjust = "none" gives the unadjusted p-values, and any method of stats::p.adjust() is accepted. A term-level test ("partial_f", "partial_chi2") counts once per outcome, in a family of its own.

table_regression() leaves the coefficients of one model unadjusted by default, each testing its own hypothesis. One exposure tested on several outcomes is the other case its help names, the design with several endpoints, where the adjustment is the convention: see Multiple-comparison adjustment there.

Intercepts

Hidden by default: each model has its own intercept, which says nothing about the exposure. show_intercept = TRUE shows them, and the table then gives each outcome a block of rows, headed by the outcome, opening with its model's (Intercept) row.

Refused

nested, layout, keep, drop, factor_layout = "flat", outcome_labels, standardized, the AME columns, show_columns = "none" and a survey design are refused, each with what to do instead; so are an exposure that is also an outcome or a covariate, and a single outcome (use table_regression()).

See also

table_regression_uv() for one outcome and several candidate predictors, table_regression() for models fitted beforehand.

Examples

# A numeric exposure: one row per outcome.
table_regression_outcomes(
  sochealth,
  outcomes   = c(wellbeing_score, bmi, life_sat_health),
  exposure   = age,
  covariates = sex
)
#> Linear regression of each outcome on age
#> 
#>  Outcome         │  N     B       95% CI        p   
#> ─────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────
#>  wellbeing_score │ 1200  0.04  [-0.02, 0.10]   .327 
#>  bmi             │ 1188  0.04  [ 0.02, 0.05]  <.001 
#>  life_sat_health │ 1192  0.00  [-0.00, 0.01]   .647 
#> 
#> Note. Linear regression models. One model per outcome, fitted separately. Adjusted for sex. Each model is fit on its own complete cases; N varies by outcome (1188–1200). Std. errors: classical (OLS). P-values adjusted across the 3 outcomes for 3 tests (Holm method). CI = confidence interval.

# A factor exposure: one block of levels per outcome.
table_regression_outcomes(
  sochealth,
  outcomes   = c(wellbeing_score, bmi),
  exposure   = employment_status,
  covariates = c(age, sex),
  labels     = TRUE
)
#> Linear regression of each outcome on Employment status
#> 
#>  Outcome                        │  N      B        95% CI        p   
#> ────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────
#>  WHO-5 wellbeing index (0-100): │ 1200                               
#>    Employed (ref.)              │         –          –          –    
#>    Student                      │        0.99  [-1.78,  3.75]  1.000 
#>    Unemployed                   │       -3.82  [-6.37, -1.27]   .020 
#>    Inactive                     │        0.14  [-2.83,  3.11]  1.000 
#>  Body mass index:               │ 1188                               
#>    Employed (ref.)              │         –          –          –    
#>    Student                      │       -0.07  [-0.74,  0.59]  1.000 
#>    Unemployed                   │        0.14  [-0.48,  0.75]  1.000 
#>    Inactive                     │        0.16  [-0.55,  0.88]  1.000 
#> 
#> Note. Linear regression models. One model per outcome, fitted separately. Adjusted for Age (years) and Sex. Each model is fit on its own complete cases; N varies by outcome (1188–1200). Std. errors: classical (OLS). P-values adjusted across the 2 outcomes for 6 tests (Holm method). CI = confidence interval.

# A binary outcome in a logistic model, beside two linear ones: its
# odds ratio next to their coefficients.
table_regression_outcomes(
  sochealth,
  outcomes     = c(wellbeing_score, bmi, smoking),
  exposure     = age,
  covariates   = sex,
  family       = list(smoking = binomial()),
  exponentiate = TRUE
)
#> Regression of each outcome on age
#> 
#>  Outcome             │  N    Estimate     95% CI        p   
#> ─────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────
#>  wellbeing_score (B) │ 1200      0.04  [-0.02, 0.10]   .327 
#>  bmi (B)             │ 1188      0.04  [ 0.02, 0.05]  <.001 
#>  smoking (OR)        │ 1175      1.01  [ 1.00, 1.01]   .327 
#> 
#> Note. wellbeing_score, bmi: linear regression; smoking: logistic regression. One model per outcome, fitted separately. Adjusted for sex. smoking: coefficients exponentiated and displayed as OR; CI bounds exponentiated. Each model is fit on its own complete cases; N varies by outcome (1175–1200). Std. errors: wellbeing_score, bmi: classical (OLS); smoking: classical (Fisher information). P-values adjusted across the 3 outcomes for 3 tests (Holm method). CI = confidence interval.
